title: Serial Schedule
description: Trace complete transaction orders, compare noncommuting results, count valid permutations, and distinguish serial execution from serializability and business correctness.

questions.question_text: What defines a serial schedule of T1 and T2?
options: T1 and T2 execute simultaneously on different CPU cores
One transaction's operations all complete before the other transaction's first operation begins — no interleaving at all
T1 and T2 both commit at exactly the same time
T1 and T2 read the same initial values
questions.explanation: A serial schedule has zero overlap in time between transactions — one runs to completion (commit or abort) before the next starts.

questions.question_text: Using the running example (A=1000, B=2000), what is the final value of A after the serial schedule <T1, T2>?
questions.explanation: T1 first reduces A to 900 (1000-100) and commits; T2 then applies 10% interest to 900, giving 990.

questions.question_text: Why do the serial schedules <T1, T2> and <T2, T1> produce different final balances for A and B?
options: One of the two schedules must be incorrect
Because the order of operations changes what value each transaction's calculation is based on — T2's interest is computed on a different base depending on whether T1 already withdrew ₹100
Serial schedules never actually change any values
Because COMMIT changes the semantics of R and W
questions.explanation: Whichever transaction runs second operates on the value left behind by the first, so different orders legitimately yield different (but each individually correct) final states.

questions.question_text: Why is serial execution a correctness reference when each transaction is correct in isolation on an appropriate valid state?
options: It always maximizes the final balance
No transaction observes another transaction’s partial execution, so the assumed isolated correctness can be composed in the chosen order
It always uses fewer CPU cycles
It replaces every application precondition
questions.explanation: The conclusion assumes correct individual transactions and a domain-valid order; serial execution cannot repair faulty logic.

questions.question_text: What is the main drawback of always using serial schedules in a production DBMS?
options: They are mathematically impossible to construct
They produce incorrect results
They give up all the throughput/response-time benefits of interleaving, since every other transaction must wait idle even if it touches unrelated data
They cannot be logged for recovery
questions.explanation: Forcing transactions to run strictly one-at-a-time means the system can never overlap one transaction's I/O wait with another's useful work, badly hurting throughput.

questions.question_text: With 3 transactions T1, T2, T3, how many distinct serial schedules (orderings) are possible?
questions.explanation: The number of serial schedules of n transactions is n! — for 3 transactions, 3! = 6.

questions.question_text: Is a schedule where T1 and T2 touch completely disjoint data items, but interleave in time, considered a serial schedule?
options: Yes, because there's no risk of interference
No — 'serial' is defined purely by timing (no overlap), regardless of whether the data accessed overlaps
Yes, because disjoint data always implies seriality
It depends on which data items are involved
questions.explanation: Seriality is about time ordering, not data overlap — if operations interleave in time at all, the schedule is non-serial even if perfectly safe.

questions.question_text: In serializability theory, what role does a serial schedule play?
options: It is irrelevant — only non-serial schedules matter
It serves as the reference standard: a non-serial schedule is judged correct precisely when it is equivalent to some serial schedule
It is used only for deadlock detection
It replaces the need for a precedence graph
questions.explanation: The entire theory of serializability (conflict and view) is about comparing an interleaved schedule against the gold-standard of some serial ordering of the same transactions.

questions.question_text: Can two serial orders produce different final values?
options: Yes, noncommuting operations can depend on order
No, serial means identical results
Only if a primary key is missing
Only after an abort
questions.explanation: Serial execution prevents interleaving, not order dependence.

questions.question_text: If the fixed transfer is changed to 200 before the same 10% increase from A=1000, B=2000, what is the final pair?
questions.explanation: The changed transfer first gives 800 and 2200; the increase then gives 880 and 2420.

questions.question_text: What is the T2-then-T1 final pair?
questions.explanation: The increase creates 1100 and 2200 before subtracting and adding 100.

questions.question_text: Does serial execution fix a wrong calculation inside one transaction?
options: Yes, automatically
Only for integer values
No
Only with two sessions
questions.explanation: Individual transaction correctness remains an assumption to establish.

questions.question_text: What does serializable allow that serial excludes?
options: Wrong ownership checks
Unbounded duplicate effects
Ignoring transaction program order
Operation interleaving with the required serial equivalence
questions.explanation: Serializability concerns equivalence rather than literal adjacency of whole executions.

questions.question_text: An A-only transaction interleaves with a B-only transaction. Is the list serial?
options: No
Yes, because values are unrelated
Only if both commit
Only when A is numeric
questions.explanation: The definition uses operation interleaving, independent of conflict absence.

questions.question_text: For three distinct transactions with the requirement T1 before T2, how many serial orders satisfy that constraint?
options: Six
Three
Two
One
questions.explanation: The valid orders are T1, T2, T3; T1, T3, T2; and T3, T1, T2. The ordering requirement excludes the other three permutations.

questions.question_text: What changes if T1 must precede T2?
options: The dependency disappears under serial execution
Every request must succeed
Some otherwise possible permutations are inadmissible
All histories become identical
questions.explanation: Domain prerequisites constrain permissible orders.

questions.question_text: Does equal final total prove equal per-item results?
options: Yes, for all transactions
Only if there are two columns
Only under autocommit
No
questions.explanation: Different pairs can sum to the same total.

questions.question_text: Does one connection imply one transaction for its entire lifetime?
options: No
Yes, always
Only if it uses SELECT
Only with a primary key
questions.explanation: A session can execute multiple independent transactions.

questions.question_text: Why can global one-at-a-time execution waste capacity?
options: It removes all indexes
Unrelated work can wait while the active transaction performs I/O
It makes arithmetic invalid
It prevents every commit
questions.explanation: Concurrency can overlap eligible independent work.

questions.question_text: Which assumption supports serial histories as a correctness reference?
options: Every transaction has the same SQL text
Every result contains the same total
Each transaction preserves required invariants in appropriate valid states
Every connection uses the same display name
questions.explanation: Seriality does not establish the correctness of transaction logic itself.

notes:
## Execute whole transactions without interleaving

A serial schedule places all operations of one transaction before the operations of the next, with no interleaving between their executions. For two completed transactions T1 and T2, the possible orders are T1 followed by T2 or T2 followed by T1. Serial describes the execution arrangement. It does not say that the transactions are identical, commute, touch the same rows or produce the same final state in both orders.

A schedule preserves each transaction's internal program order. If T1 reads A, computes a change and writes A, the schedule cannot move its write before that required read merely to obtain a convenient result. When studying serial reference histories, include transaction boundaries and outcomes explicitly. An operation list without a clear indication of which transaction owns each operation is not enough to establish that complete transaction executions are contiguous.

## Trace a transfer and a percentage adjustment

Use the familiar two-item example with A initially one thousand and B initially two thousand. T1 transfers one hundred from A to B. T2 applies a ten-percent increase to each current value. Treat the quantities as exact arithmetic for the demonstration; a real monetary or points system must separately define its numeric types, rounding and authorization rules. The example studies operation order rather than recommending a financial policy.

```text
T1: read A; A := A - 100; write A;
    read B; B := B + 100; write B; commit
T2: read A; A := A * 1.10; write A;
    read B; B := B * 1.10; write B; commit
```

In order T1 then T2, the transfer produces A equal to nine hundred and B equal to two thousand one hundred. T2 then increases those current values to nine hundred ninety and two thousand three hundred ten. Both transactions obtain complete predecessor results rather than partial work from an overlapping transaction. The final pair is therefore 990 and 2310.

In order T2 then T1, the increase first produces 1100 and 2200. The subsequent transfer produces 1000 and 2300. Both serial histories preserve the transaction programs, but their final pairs differ. The transfer and percentage adjustment do not commute. An application requiring one particular ordering must state and enforce that requirement; serial execution alone allows either serial order unless another dependency constrains it.

| Serial order | After first transaction | Final A | Final B |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 then T2 | A=900, B=2100 | 990 | 2310 |
| T2 then T1 | A=1100, B=2200 | 1000 | 2300 |

## Explain the correctness assumption precisely

Serial execution is a useful reference model when each transaction, executed alone from an appropriate valid state, preserves the required invariants. In that setting, completing one correct transaction before beginning another avoids interference between their partial states. The qualification matters: a transaction containing an incorrect formula, missing ownership check or invalid state transition does not become correct merely because nobody else runs at the same time.

Some requirements also constrain the allowed order. A return cannot validly precede creation of the loan it returns. A transaction can reject an operation whose preconditions do not hold in the state it encounters. The serial reference need not mean every submitted request succeeds. Include the actual success, denial or abort outcome when deciding whether a history satisfies the application's intended behavior.

The two-item arithmetic also shows the limits of checking only a total. Both serial final pairs sum to three thousand three hundred, even though the individual values differ. A nonserial history could conceivably match that same total while violating the required per-item result or exposing an unfinished write. Aggregate equality is useful evidence for one invariant, not a complete proof that two transaction histories are equivalent.

## Distinguish serial from serializable

A serializable schedule may interleave transaction operations while remaining equivalent to an appropriate serial schedule under the chosen equivalence definition. Conflict serializability preserves the ordering of conflicting operations on the same item. View serializability preserves read sources, initial reads and final writers under its model. Neither term means the physical operation list has no interleaving.

For example, T1 can read and update only A while T2 reads and updates only unrelated B. Their operations may interleave without creating a conflicting dependency between the transactions. That interleaved list is still nonserial by definition, even when it is conflict equivalent to both serial orders. Disjoint data access explains harmless interleaving; it does not change the definition of serial.

Conversely, a shared-item interleaving can create dependency edges in both directions. A conflict cycle rules out conflict serializability even if the final values look plausible on one fixture. Trace operations and their dependencies instead of classifying by the number of rows or by whether the application happened to report success. The relevant proof concerns the complete execution history and its stated abstraction.

## Count orders without ignoring external constraints

For n distinct transactions that can be freely ordered, there are n factorial possible serial permutations. Three transactions have six orders: T1, T2, T3; T1, T3, T2; T2, T1, T3; T2, T3, T1; T3, T1, T2; and T3, T2, T1. This count concerns transaction orders, not the potentially much larger number of operation-level interleavings.

If an external rule requires T1 before T2, some permutations become inadmissible. A request that depends on a previously produced identifier cannot simply be placed before its prerequisite and assumed to succeed identically. Distinguish the combinatorial count of unconstrained serial orders from the number of domain-valid successful histories. Also keep transaction identity distinct from identical SQL text: separate requests remain separate transactions even when they execute the same template.

## Understand the concurrency trade-off

Running every transaction globally one at a time can leave useful work waiting while the current transaction performs I/O or touches unrelated data. Interleaving allows the server to overlap eligible work and improve throughput or response time under suitable conditions. The benefit is workload-dependent; a heavily contended resource still requires coordination, and additional concurrency can increase waiting or retries rather than improve performance indefinitely.

A serial reference model is therefore a reasoning tool, not necessarily a recommendation to put a single global application lock around the database. Existing database concurrency control can preserve a required isolation model while exploiting independent work. Measure the actual workload and keep transactions short, but do not remove necessary coordination merely because a serialized fixture appears slower.

## Keep transactions, sessions and statements distinct

One connection can execute many transactions sequentially. Multiple connections can submit work whose actual execution is serialized by contention or scheduling. Two statements next to each other in application code may nevertheless commit independently under autocommit, so they do not automatically form one indivisible transaction. Identify database boundaries rather than inferring them from a function name or a visual grouping in an editor.

Read-only operations and aborted attempts also deserve explicit treatment. A read-only transaction can observe an invalid partial state under an insufficient concurrency contract even if it never changes a row. An aborted transaction can release resources and leave recovery work to the engine. A simplified completed-write schedule is useful for teaching, but state what the abstraction omits before drawing conclusions about a real service's behavior.

Before drawing a comparison, label the initial state and the exact successful transaction outcomes. This prevents accidentally comparing one committed history with another history that omitted a failed attempt.

## Solve two schedule exercises

First exercise: recompute the two arithmetic orders from the specified starting values. The solutions are 990/2310 and 1000/2300. Explain why their equal total does not make the pairs identical and why neither order alone proves the application chose the required business ordering. Then change the fixed transfer to two hundred and repeat the calculations using the same transaction programs and exact arithmetic assumptions.

Second exercise: write an interleaving where T1 touches only A and T2 touches only B, then group each transaction's operations into both serial orders. The interleaving is nonserial, while absence of cross-transaction conflicts makes the orders conflict equivalent in the stated item model. Continue with [nonserial schedules](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/non-serial-schedule), [conflict serializability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/conflict-serializability) and [transaction boundaries](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-boundaries) to connect the reference model to actual transaction design.
